target.Title: 6 Ways People Become Rich With Debt

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Diego just signed papers putting himself
another $200,000
into debt, and he did it grinning like
he'd won something. His bank account
didn't shrink. His net worth just went
up. Meanwhile, three doors down, Curtis
hasn't owed a soul a dollar in 9 years,
checks his perfect credit score like
it's a lottery ticket, and is quietly,
slowly going broke standing still.

Bad debt buys things that
lose value and drain your account every
month. Good debt buys things that either
climb in value or pay you to own them.

According to Federal Reserve data, the
wealthiest households carry far less
debt relative to what they own, around
12% for the top sliver, versus well over
60% for a typical middle-class family.
The rich borrow less proportionally and
get richer doing it.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: 12%/over60%notverifiedwithdefinedyear,wealthgroups,ratioformula. Debt/assets differs debt/networth and medianratio differs ratioofaggregatelevels. Correlationcannotshowborrowingcausedwealth.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Hold on to that question because
it ends up being worth roughly eight
times Curtis's net worth.

The first way is real estate, and it's
first for a reason. It's the most
accessible serious leverage a normal
person can actually get their hands on.

He puts 20% down and the bank
covers the rest. But, and this is the
part that breaks people's brains, he
keeps 100% of the appreciation. Put
numbers on it. The property costs
$250,000.
Diego puts down 50,000. It rises a
modest 5% in a year, $12,500.
If he'd paid all cash, that's a 5%
return.
Fine, boring, but he didn't pay cash. He
put in 50,000, so 12,500
is a 25% return. Same house, same year,
same market, he multiplied his return by
five using the bank's money.

And that's before the tenant shows up
and starts paying down his mortgage
every month with their own paycheck.
Fast forward 10 years on that single
property. It's worth around 340,000.
The loan's down to about uh 166,000,
and Diego's equity, his slice, is
roughly 180,000.
His original 50 grand turned into 180
largely on somebody else's income.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: The stated rounded inputs give 340K−166K=174K, not exactly180K; because all three values are approximate this is a 6K reconciliation gap, not proof the actual scenario is false. 250Kto340Kin10y implies3.1226%annual; continued5%wouldgive407223.66, but the narrator only explicitly assumes5% for the first year. Loanbalance166K cannot be reproduced withoutAPR/term; own6%30ycase gives167371.45. Tenant rent is gross revenue, not net mortgage coverage.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
That same multiplier runs in reverse. If
the house drops 20% instead of rising,
Diego's entire $50,000 down payment is
gone, wiped, and that's not a
hypothetical. It's a documentary, it's
called 2008. When millions of
over-leveraged owners watched their
equity evaporate while the bank came
knocking anyway.

Diego can even refinance,
pull his original 50,000 back out
tax-free, a loan isn't income, and run
it again with the same money. Investors
have a name for that loop, they call it
BRRRR buy, rehab, rent, refinance,
repeat. Diego buys a beat-up place
cheap, fixes it up until it's worth
more, rents it out,
then refinances against the new higher
value and pulls his original cash right
back out to go again. Same 50 grand
recycled into a second house, then a
third. He's not saving up for each
property, he's reusing one down payment
on a loop. Meanwhile, Curtis is saving
up to buy one rental outright in cash
sometime around his 65th birthday. By
then, Diego owns six of them.

Businesses fail, a lot of them,
roughly half within 5 years and 2/3
within 10.

here's why this is still the mechanism
that mints more everyday millionaires
than almost anything else.

The Small Business Administration backs
loans that let a regular person buy a
cash-flowing business with as little as
10% down. Picture a boring, unglamorous
winner, a laundromat, a plumbing outfit,
a pest control route that earns $200,000
a year and sells for $800,000. Diego
doesn't need $800,000. He needs about
80
He borrows the rest, and then the
business's own profit pays back the
loan. Sit with that because it's the
whole game. The asset pays for itself.
Diego puts in 80,000, and the thing he
bought generates the money that clears
the debt he bought it with. Loan gone,
he owns an $800,000 cash machine
outright for a tenth of the sticker.

This, scaled up with billions and much
better suits, is exactly what private
equity does. Leveraged buyout is just a
fancy phrase for borrow most of the
money, buy the company, let the company
pay off its own purchase. They call it a
strategy. It's the same hustle.

Buying an existing, profitable business
tilts the odds your way versus starting
from zero.
You're buying proven cash flow instead
of a hope and a logo.

But tilts the odds isn't guarantees, and
if that laundromat's revenue dries up,
the loan payment shows up anyway every
month with the patience of a serial
killer.

So, say his portfolio is
now worth $5 million
and he originally put in $1 million. If
he sells to get cash, he owes capital
gains tax on the $4 million in profit, a
bill somewhere around $950,000.
Almost a million gone just for touching
his own money.

The bank hands
him a loan at say 6% using the portfolio
as collateral. On $3 million borrowed,
that's $180,000
a year in interest. Line those two
numbers up. $950,000
in tax if he sells versus $180,000
in interest if he borrows.
And the kicker, his $5 million stays
fully invested and growing while he
spends the borrowed cash. He uses his
wealth without selling it, without
triggering the tax, without stepping out
of the market.

Borrowed money isn't
income, so there's no tax on it at all.
Then the morbid last step, the die part.
When Diego passes, his heirs inherit the
stock, and thanks to a rule called the
step-up in basis,
that $4 million in gains he never paid
tax on simply vanishes. Legally, the
slate wipes clean, the estate settles
the loan, the family keeps the rest, and
the taxman never got his slice.

It's how people like
Larry Ellison and Elon Musk operate,
pledging billions in shares as
collateral instead of selling.

Should you with a normal portfolio go
lever up on margin this afternoon?
Please know, this one has teeth.
If the market crashes and your
collateral drops, you get a margin call,
the bank demanding its money back at the
exact worst moment, forcing you to sell
into the crash, which is the financial
equivalent of being asked to bail water
while someone drills fresh holes in the
boat.
But the principle underneath is worth
stealing. To the rich, selling is a last
resort. Borrowing is the first move.

The
logic, if Diego's mortgage is locked at
3% and the stock market historically
returns around 10.
Then every dollar he doesn't throw at
paying the mortgage off early and
invests instead, earns him the gap.
Borrow at three, earn at 10. That
seven-point spread is basically free
money on paper. It's why financially
sophisticated people are weirdly in no
hurry to kill a low-interest mortgage.

Curtis hurled every spare dollar at his
3% loan because, in his words, debt bad.
Diego kept the cheap loan and invested
the difference, and across 30 years that
one choice is worth a small fortune. It
only works, mind you, if you actually
stay invested through the ugly years
instead of panic selling at the bottom.
The spread pays the patient and finds
the twitchy.

inflation quietly
pays off your debt for you. Diego
borrows a fixed amount today, his
mortgage payment is locked the same
number every month for 30 years. But
inflation makes every dollar worth a
little less as time rolls on. His salary
rises, rents rise, the price of a
sandwich rises, and that mortgage
payment just sits there.
Frozen, getting easier to cover every
single year. He's repaying tomorrow's
expensive loan with money that keeps
getting cheaper. Picture a $2,000
monthly payment. In year one, it takes a
real bite out of his paycheck. But, 30
years later, after decades of raises and
rising prices, that same $2,000 is what
he leaves as a tip at a nice dinner. The
number on the bill never moved, the
world around it inflated, and the debt
shrank in real terms every year he did
absolutely nothing.

The Federal Reserve has studied this
outright. Inflation quietly transfers
wealth from lenders to borrowers. The
lender loses, the fixed-rate borrower
wins. And the single biggest winner from
the whole mechanism? The US
government perched on tens of trillions
of dollars in fixed-rate debt that
inflation melts down like an ice
sculpture at a wedding. If it's good
enough for the Treasury, it's worth a
second look.

The interest on your credit card and
your car loan, not deductible. You eat
that cost alone in the dark. The
interest on a business loan or an
investment property, deductible. The
government chips in. Same act, borrow
money, pay interest, but the code treats
consumer debt like a vice and productive
debt like a virtue.
So, when you're paying interest on that
financed truck, you swallow the whole
bill. When Diego pays interest on his
rental, he writes it off, which quietly
makes his real borrowing cost lower than
the rate printed on the page.

Then there's the crown jewel,
depreciation. On that rental, the tax
code lets Diego deduct a chunk of the
building's value every year as if it's
wearing out, even though the place is in
reality going up in value.
On a $275,000
building, that's around $10,000 a year
in deductions he claims without spending
a real dollar.

If
Diego's in a 30% tax bracket and between
deductible interest and depreciation,
he's got $20,000 in write-offs, that's
$6,000 the government simply doesn't
collect from him every single year for
owning an asset that's climbing in value
the whole time. Curtis, paying interest
on his car, gets exactly none of that.
He writes the check and moves on.

Recent
law made it sharper. As of the 2025
legislation, businesses can once again
write off 100% of certain purchases in
the first year, a provision called bonus
depreciation that had been fading out
and got fully restored.
Pair it with a strategy called cost
segregation and serious real estate
investors front-load enormous
deductions, sometimes zeroing out their
taxable income the very year they buy.

Which brings us finally to the sixth
way, less a tactic than the idea sitting
under the other five. Every one of those
plays is really the same move. Use other
people's money to control an asset you
couldn't buy outright and let the asset
do the heavy lifting.
Real estate, businesses, portfolios,
cheap arbitrage, tax advantage loans,
strip the details and it's one motion.
Borrow, aim it at something that grows
or pays, let time compound the gap.

$40,000 borrowed for a nursing
credential that adds $30,000 a year to
your paycheck is one of the best trades
on this entire list. $40,000 borrowed
for a degree that lands you right back
at your old job is just a very expensive
participation trophy.

Then there's
seller financing where the person
selling a business lets you pay them
over time straight out of the profits.
Same principle, no bank in the room. A
franchise loan, a credit line against
equipment that earns more than it costs.
Different costume every time, one idea
underneath.

The boat you've been eyeing
is a liability, a duplex is an asset,
that watch is a liability, a profitable
business is an asset.
Rate and terms matter, but that first
question decides almost everything.

You can do all of this correctly
and still lose.
We love the people who leverage their
way to a fortune and quietly forget the
ones who leveraged their way into a
crater.
For every Diego, there's a shadow Diego
who bought at the wrong time, borrowed
too much, hit a bad stretch, and got
flattened.

Research shows more than half of
individual stocks actually lose money
over their entire lifetime.

Even the man who built the whole debt is
dumb gospel, Curtis lives by built it
after personally going bankrupt from
real estate leverage in his 20s.

Four conditions and a good debt play
needs all four. One, the spread has to
be real. The thing you buy has to
reasonably out-earn the loan.
Two, it has to be an appreciating or
cash-flowing asset, not a depreciating
toy wearing an investment costume.
Three, the leverage has to be survivable
with enough cushion that a bad year
bends you instead of snapping you. And
four, you have to keep making the
payments through the rough patches
because the rough patches always come
and a loan, unlike you, never gets
tired, never sleeps in, and never once
feels bad about it.
Miss any one of the four and good debt
quietly turns back into the kind that's
trying to kill you.

That 30,000 he kept so
safe in savings,
a decade later it had crept up to about
34,000, and after inflation took its
cut, it actually bought less than the
day he first parked it. He guarded that
money so carefully, it quietly shrank in
his hands.

Diego took the same instinct, aimed it
at assets instead, and turned $150,000
down payment into $180,000
in equity, then did it five more times.
Same street. Same paycheck. Same
starting line.

One of them retired at 50
with six properties and a business that
runs without him. The other has a
paid-off house, a flawless credit score,
and a quiet
nagging sense that he did everything
right and somehow still got lapped. The
difference was never courage or luck or
income. Debt is just a tool. In the
wrong hands, it's a trap that eats
people alive. In the right hands, aimed
at the right thing, it's the closest
thing to a cheat code ordinary people
are actually allowed to use.
